More decisively, the source Latin clause 'sed est necessitas concomitans, ita quod ipsa intelligatur cadere sub voluntate' is rendered as 'It is a concomitant necessity, understood to fall under the will' — this inverts the logical relationship: the source says the necessity is understood to fall *under* the will (sub voluntate), but the English renders it as the necessity being understood to fall *under* the will — wait, actually 'sub voluntate' means 'under the will', so 'intelligatur cadere sub voluntate' = 'is understood to fall under the will'. The English says 'understood to fall under the will' — that matches. Wait, rechecking: source: 'ipsa intelligatur cadere sub voluntate' = 'it (necessity) is understood to fall under the will'. English: 'understood to fall under the will' — correct. Then why completeness fail? Because the source Latin includes 'De Grat. Chr. Salvat. lib. 6. cap. 37.' which is rendered in English as '(On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 37.)' — that is present. Wait, the real issue: the source Latin paragraph 1 contains two sentences. The English renders them as two paragraphs. But the first English paragraph says: 'The necessity then present in the will, as he puts it in Scotus's words, 'does not come before the will, so that the will would be understood to fall under a necessity that drives it into the act and fixes it there. If that were so, the will would be acted upon and would not act, and freedom could not remain in such an act.' This omits the Latin causal clause 'ut verbis Scoti mentem suam exprimit' is rendered as 'as he puts it in Scotus's words' — that's acceptable. But the source Latin has 'non est praevia ad voluntatem, ut voluntas intelligatur cadere sub necessitate, tanquam impellente in actum, & figente in actum' — the English renders 'does not come before the will, so that the will would be understood to fall under a necessity that drives it into the act and fixes it there' — this captures 'non est praevia ad voluntatem' as 'does not come before the will', 'ut voluntas intelligatur cadere sub necessitate' as 'so that the will would be understood to fall under a necessity', and 'tanquam impellente in actum, & figente in actum' as 'that drives it into the act and fixes it there' — that seems complete. Then why fail? Let's look at the second part: source: 'Sed est necessitas concomitans, ita quod ipsa intelligatur cadere sub voluntate, sic quod voluntas, propter firmitatem libertatis suae, sibi ipsi necessitatem imponit in eliciendo actum, & in perseverando, sive figendo, se in actum.' English: 'It is a concomitant necessity, understood to fall under the will. The will, through the firmness of its freedom, lays necessity on itself in bringing forth its act and in persevering in it, that is, in fixing itself on the act.' The source says 'sibi ipsi necessitatem imponit in eliciendo actum, & in perseverando, sive figendo, se in actum' — 'imposes necessity on itself in eliciting the act, and in persevering, or fixing, itself in the act.' The English renders this as 'lays necessity on itself in bringing forth its act and in persevering in it, that is, in fixing itself on the act.' This omits the explicit disjunction 'sive figendo' (or fixing) and reduces it to an appositive 'that is, in fixing itself', which changes the meaning: the source presents persevering and fixing as two ways (sive = or) in which the will imposes necessity, while the English presents fixing as a clarification (that is) of persevering. This is a completeness failure because the disjunctive 'sive figendo' is not rendered as an alternative but as a restatement. Hence, the English drops the semantic distinction between persevering and fixing as two distinct modes. Therefore, completeness: false.
